newsitem.title: UK: LME copper ends up, spreads flare in thin trading.
newsitem.headline: LME copper ends up, spreads flare in thin trading.

text.p: Copper prices ended modestly firmer in uninspired trading on Tuesday afternoon, joined by most of the other London Metal Exchange (LME) base metals.
Widening backwardation in the copper market was the main feature in otherwise thin, quiet trading, traders said.
Three months delivery copper ended the kerb at $2,286 per tonne, up a modest $8 from Monday's kerb close.
But the cash to threes backwardation flared out after starting at around $60 in the morning, and ended the kerb at $72/$82.
Despite the passing of Third Wednesday pricing on Monday, some traders said, the recent technical tightness which pushed cash/threes backwardation above $300 in recent weeks may not be over.
Borrowing has emerged in March and early April, which suggested that some short positions may have been rolled over, they added.
The widening spreads, along with a small drawdown in stocks provided support for copper. On the upside, the $2,313 level from November 28 last year remains the target to breach.
One physical traded predicted that cash/threes would settle in a $60-$80 backwardation.
"There is still a great deal of nervousness ...stocks are relatively low and vulnerable. Nobody wants to be short in case tightness reappears," he said.
On a fundamental level, traders were watching for a spike in Chinese demand for base metals as the holiday season ended.
However, so far any sizable Chinese business was absent from the market, traders said.
Aluminium, helped by a 5,050-tonne decline in stocks, ended at its highs and $14 firmer at $1,584 per tonne.
Nickel finished sharply lower at $7,665, down $85. An attempt to bounce from its lows failed and prices resumed drifting lower.
Lead, which boosted by a stocks decline, was $2 up at $657.
Zinc was slightly easier at $1,213, down $6.50, following a stocks rise of 1,125 tonnes.
Tin, helped by a modest drawdown of 95 tonnes, ended $40 firmer at $6,065.
